passages.label: Text 1
passages.text: The geographer Andrew Sharp argued that the spread of people across the Pacific is better explained by accident than by intention. The islands of Polynesia, he noted, lie hundreds or thousands of miles apart, often below the horizon until a vessel is nearly upon them. Without compasses, charts, or written records, he reasoned, ancient voyagers could not have held a deliberate course across such distances or reliably found a particular island and then sailed home from it. The settlement of the Pacific, on Sharp's account, was the work of canoes blown off course or carried by currents, their landfalls a matter of chance rather than of planned, two-way exploration.

passages.label: Text 2
passages.text: The anthropologist Ben Finney accepted that Polynesian voyagers carried none of the instruments European sailors relied on, but he drew the opposite conclusion. Traditional navigators, he argued, fixed direction by the rising and setting points of particular stars, read the long ocean swells that bend around islands, and watched seabirds returning to land at dusk—an integrated body of knowledge that needed no writing to be exact. To test whether such methods could sustain deliberate voyages, Finney helped build a double-hulled canoe, the Hōkūleʻa, and sailed it from Hawaii to Tahiti and back with no instruments, guided only by a traditional navigator. The crossing, he contended, showed that the dispersal Sharp attributed to chance lay well within the reach of intentional wayfinding.

question: Based on the texts, how would Finney (Text 2) most likely respond to the claim presented in Text 1?

choices.text: He would accept that Polynesian voyagers carried no instruments yet argue that the star paths, swells, and returning seabirds they tracked made deliberate two-way voyaging possible.
He would dispute Sharp's assumption that the islands of Polynesia lie far enough apart for the distances between them to have posed any real obstacle to early canoes.
He would concede that the settlement of the Pacific was largely accidental but propose that only its final stages involved any deliberate navigation.
He would question whether canoes of the kind available to ancient voyagers could have stayed seaworthy across open water for as long as such crossings required.

explanation: The correct answer is A. Sharp's case rests on the absence of instruments: without compasses or charts, he holds, deliberate long-distance voyaging was impossible, so settlement must have been accidental. Finney grants the very premise—Polynesians had no such instruments—but rejects the conclusion, because the star paths, swells, and seabird cues he describes (and the instrument-free Hōkūleʻa voyage he sailed to demonstrate them) show that precise, intentional navigation did not depend on instruments at all. B has Finney quarrel with the distances, a point he never disputes; C has him accept the accidental account he sets out to overturn; and D raises a seaworthiness worry that appears nowhere in his argument.
